why: The policy describes a yearly requirements process, but the requirements list it relies on is not in the bundle.
The policy was approved by management on 14 July 2026, as the publication record confirms.
The policy has Purpose and Objectives sections covering the significance of security and its aims.
The intranet export shows the policies published under Security, viewed by 163 of 171 employees.
Four change notices were sent to employees and suppliers via the portal, with recipient counts.
The policy says requirements come from the business plan, contracts and law, but no yearly record of that work is in the bundle.
No document states consequences for non-conformance.
Ten supporting standards and procedures exist, are listed in the policy and are published.
The yearly policy review is recorded, but the encryption standard is past its yearly review (approved 2022).
The procedure defines reportable events across personnel, physical, IT and supplier topics, published and taught in training.
Email, ticket and hotline channels are defined, were used for 43 reports, and are covered in training.
Email, ticket, hotline and feedback channels exist and were used in practice.
The security desk is named as the single point of contact for all reports.
An urgent hotline and asynchronous email or ticket channels are defined and used, with 12 hotline reports.
Reporting is an employment duty, the basic course covers it, and 166 of 171 employees completed it.
A supplier report was accepted and processed, but no channel for external parties is documented.
The intranet and posters reach employees, but nothing shows suppliers can see how to report.
A two-working-day feedback step is defined, and the register records feedback for all 43 reports.
Reports are recorded within one working day, with a median first action of 3 hours.
Actions were taken, but no review is recorded for high incident 2026-007 or critical incident 2026-031.
Lessons led to a USB block and a briefing, but the required reviews of high and critical incidents are missing.
Each event in the register has a category, type and priority.
Owners per category, coordination by the information security officer and named deputies are defined.
No strategy for reporting potentially criminal aspects to authorities is in the bundle.
166 of 171 employees completed the basic course, and all 12 new joiners did so within a month.
The concept covers most listed topics but not compliance issues or external IT services.
Administrators, managers, customer-network staff and prototype areas are named target groups, with sessions attended.
Management approved the concept on 16 February 2026.
The course runs yearly, and an event briefing after incident 2026-007 was sent and read by 158 people.
Course completions and target-group session attendance are recorded.
The concept says contacts are named in courses and on the intranet, but no record shows employees know them.
The standard picks sign-in per system from its exposure, and the rollout record shows it applied.
The standard follows national authority guidance, and 12-character passwords with second factors are in place.
Authentication procedures are defined per system and enforced, with dates in the rollout record.
The directory enforces a 12-character minimum and a breached-password check.
All 9 administrator accounts are separate and use hardware keys since 15 April 2026.
Account creation, change and deletion run through tickets, with 12 joiners, 7 movers and 9 leavers recorded.
The one-person-one-account rule applies, and the review found every employee account belongs to a current employee.
Shared accounts are limited to one display terminal type, but the account register that lists them is not in the bundle.
Employee leavers were disabled on their last day, but three supplier accounts stayed active after their jobs ended.
A six-monthly account review for H1 2026 is recorded across employee, admin, supplier and technical accounts.
The procedure bans email and requires in-person or own-phone handover, but no record shows how details were handed over.
The login-information rules cover disclosure, writing down, change on suspicion, reuse and first-login change, and the settings are in place.
New accounts start with the standard employee role, as the joiner tickets show.
No record shows that manufacturer default accounts and passwords were disabled.
Each joiner ticket shows the system owner approved the account before it was created.
The procedure requires a second-person approval, and every joiner ticket shows one.
The procedure requires provider accounts to be disabled at job end, but three supplier accounts were found still active.
Deadlines are defined (end of last working day, deletion after 90 days), with leaver examples.
The breached-password check blocks known passwords, but default-password blocking is not stated.
Authenticator apps and hardware keys are in place, but nothing shows the second-factor medium is protected.
Internal accounts are reviewed, but accounts in customer systems were excluded from the review.
No record shows interactive login for service accounts is technically blocked.
The policy sets approval and least privilege, but the review found 11 rights left over from earlier role changes.
Internal rights are reviewed six-monthly, but customer-system rights were excluded from the review.
The policy sets out how access is authorised, starting from no access.
Rights are bundled into 14 roles, each with an owner, and the roles were reviewed.
Access follows the job role and is approved by the system owner before IT grants it.
Ordinary accounts never hold admin rights, and administrators use separate accounts.
A mover ticket shows same-day change, but 11 rights from earlier role changes had not been removed.
The standard names approved methods and key lengths, but it is past its yearly review; the 2026 TLS scan supports it.
The concept covers methods and key lifecycle, but it is past its yearly review and no implementation record is in the bundle.
Internal and outside transfer services are listed with owners and classification limits.
Rules by classification are defined, and the register records the highest class each service may carry.
No remote access, encrypted transfer and logged downloads from the platform are recorded.
No record of measures for correct addressing or transfer is in the bundle.
Confidential files need platform or end-to-end encryption, and the TLS scan confirms transport encryption.
Logging rules are set, and the scope list applies them to each system.
Sign-ins, failed sign-ins, rights changes and admin actions are logged for each in-scope system.
The scope list was checked on 9 March 2026, and the canteen screen was judged not to need logging.
Providers' monitoring options are listed, but the register says none was considered when the services were approved.
Monthly reviews for June to September 2026 are recorded, and findings were escalated.
Escalation to the security desk is defined and was used for findings 2026-028 and 2026-039.
The standard says other admins cannot change central logs, but no record tests this.
Sign-in, download and rights logs exist, but mail filter alerts are unwatched and no network monitoring record exists.
Advisories are gathered nightly from manufacturers and CVE, and scored with CVSS 3.1.
Each tracked CVE is mapped to its affected assets and given a priority.
Each tracked risk has a treatment: closed patch tickets, a scheduled update, or risk acceptance RA-2026-03.
Patch tickets show work was done, but no patch management procedure is in the bundle.
The CAD vault server is limited to the design VLAN with logged downloads under RA-2026-03.
Patch tickets are closed, but no installation check is recorded and one ERP update is overdue.
No backup concept is in the bundle.
No recovery concept is in the bundle; the one-day restore objective is a target, not a concept.
No backup and recovery concept per service is in the bundle.
